Because $q\equiv3\pmod4$, $q$ is irreducible in the Euclidean domain $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, and therefore it is prime. Thus $(q)$ is a prime ideal, so $R=\mathbb{Z}[i]/(q)$ is an integral domain. \begin{proof}
The quotient map reduces each coefficient modulo $q$, so every class in $\mathbb{Z}[i]/(q)$ has a representative $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\{0,1,\dots,q-1\}$. If two such representatives have the same class, then
\[
(a_1-a_2)+(b_1-b_2)i\in(q).
\]
Thus both coefficient differences are divisible by $q$. Since each difference lies between $-(q-1)$ and $q-1$, both differences are zero. Consequently these $q^2$ representatives are distinct, and the quotient has $q^2$ elements.

For $q\equiv3\pmod4$, the prime integer $q$ remains irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$: if $q=\alpha\beta$, then taking norms gives $q^2=N(\alpha)N(\beta)$, and a nontrivial factorization would yield an element of norm $q$, which would require a solution to $x^2+y^2=q$, impossible since a sum of two squares cannot be congruent to $3$ modulo $4$. Since $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is a Euclidean domain, irreducible elements are prime. Hence $(q)$ is prime and the quotient is an integral domain.

A finite integral domain is a field, because multiplication by any nonzero element is an injective self-map and therefore is surjective. Thus $\mathbb{Z}[i]/(q)$ is a field with $q^2$ elements.
\end{proof}
